details:
**Additive identity**
Zero is the number that leaves any number unchanged when added to it, and any number multiplied by zero gives zero. It is the only integer that is neither positive nor negative. Mathematicians disagree about whether the natural numbers should start at zero.

**Division by zero and having no reciprocal**
Zero is the only real number without a multiplicative inverse, so its reciprocal is undefined and dividing by it is undefined. Many programming languages throw an error when a program divides by zero. The function 1/x has both its horizontal and vertical asymptotes at zero.

**Zero-based array indexing**
In C, C++, and many other programming languages, the first element of an array has index 0. Edsger Dijkstra wrote a well-known note arguing that numbering should start at zero, calling it the "most natural number." Forgetting zero-based indexing can cause an off-by-one "fencepost" error.

**Boolean "false" and binary**
In Boolean logic and binary, 0 represents "false" or "off," while 1 represents "true" or "on." Together the digits 0 and 1 make up all binary values.

**Critical points and inflection points**
At a local maximum or minimum, a function's first derivative is either zero or undefined. At an inflection point, where concavity changes, the second derivative is usually zero. The derivative of a constant function is zero everywhere, since a horizontal line has zero slope.

**Conservative vector fields and the divergence of a curl**
The line integral of a conservative vector field around any closed loop equals zero, because the result depends only on the endpoints. In vector calculus, the divergence of the curl of any smooth vector field is always zero.

**Integral of an odd function**
An odd function satisfies f(−x) = −f(x), so its integral over a symmetric interval from −a to a is zero, for example the integral of sin x from −N to N. Its positive and negative areas cancel exactly.

**Standard hydrogen electrode and standard enthalpy of formation**
The standard hydrogen electrode is assigned a reduction potential of exactly zero volts and is the reference for other electrode potentials. By definition, elements in their standard states have a standard enthalpy of formation of zero.

**Oxidation number, formal charge, and neutral charge**
Uncombined free elements have an oxidation number of zero, and a neutral atom or molecule has a net charge of zero. The best Lewis structures keep each atom's formal charge as close to zero as possible.

**Zero determinant and singular matrices**
A square matrix whose determinant is zero is singular and cannot be inverted. A system of linear equations in which every equation equals zero is called homogeneous. The null space of a linear transformation is the set of vectors it sends to zero.

**Zero product property, zero divisors, and ring characteristic**
The zero product property says that if a product is zero, at least one factor is zero. Rings with this property, such as the quotient of a ring by a prime ideal, have no "zero divisors." A ring's characteristic is the smallest number of copies of 1 that add up to zero.

**Empty set**
The empty (null) set has zero elements, so its cardinality is zero, and it is a subset of every set. Two disjoint sets have an intersection with zero elements.

**Zero in computing: exit codes, hexadecimal, and signed zero**
In Bash and Unix, an exit code of 0 conventionally means a program succeeded. In C and C++, hexadecimal literals start with "0x." The IEEE 754 floating-point standard defines both a positive zero and a negative zero.

**Zeroth law of thermodynamics and absolute zero**
The zeroth law states that two systems that are each in thermal equilibrium with a third are in equilibrium with each other, which is the basis for temperature. Zero degrees Celsius is the freezing point of water. Absolute zero, 0 kelvin (−273.15 °C), is the lowest possible temperature.

**Zero in statistics and probability**
The probability of an impossible event is zero. A set of z-scores has a mean of zero, as do the residuals of a least-squares linear regression. Uncorrelated variables give an R-squared of zero, and the sample mean has a breakdown point of zero because one extreme outlier can distort it without limit.
